newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hopes of semiconductor revival lift shares in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Hopes of semiconductor revival lift shares in Asia.

text.p: Gains in semiconductor shares powered Asian stock markets on Thursday as signs that chip prices may be starting to rebound drew investors, though brokers cautioned against hopes of a substantial revival.
"High-tech shares were active on Wall Street overnight and some foreign investors think Japanese chip maker shares are a good investment," said Hiroshi Morimoto, general manager at Daiwa Securities.

Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd, said: "It is important when prices of 16 megabit DRAMs (dynamic random-access memories) stop falling as it affects chip makers' corporate results. But the (chip) market has not yet bottomed out."

Prices of 16 megabit DRAMs, widely used in personal computers as memory chips, have risen to $10 from $8 in early August. The upswing ignited hopes that a worldwide chip glut may be over, lifting high-technology share prices in New York as well as in Asia.

"The U.S. NASDAQ composite index, studded with high-tech shares, is above 1,200 now, signifying that the electronics sector is looking better and that is rubbing off on the Tokyo market," Toyo Securities strategist Haruo Nakaharu said.
Japanese chip industry leaders rose on Thursday, with NEC Corp, Toshiba CorpHitachi Ltdand Fujitsu Ltdheading the list of most heavily traded shares. Prices were up for a second straight day.
In Taiwan, another major chip producer, analysts said U.S. high-tech shares' gains gave a boost to domestic chip makers and they expected the industry to recover in the fourth quarter.
"The fourth quarter is the traditional hot sales season for electronics firms. The prospects look good for these firms," said Eric Liu of National Securities.
Expected price rises for integrated circuit chips should also boost computer companies' performance, brokers said.
Analysts and dealers in Singapore, however, were cautious over the sudden popularity of semiconductor stocks.
"We have yet to see indications from suppliers that there is indeed a turnaround," an analyst at Singapore brokerage said.

"It could be a blip," a senior institutional dealer said. "Investors are buying on the premise that traditionally the demand for the chips is up in the fourth quarter due to the Christmas season... Our house believes the global oversupply will take about two years to absorb."

Bullishness in the chip sector in Tokyo even towed semiconductor equipment firm shares higher. But in Kuala Lumpur, the sole publicly listed semiconductor-related firm, Malaysian Pacific Industries Bhd (MPI), was unmoved.
Analysts said that while the shares of the chip packaging maker were hit in July by oversupply, so far the shares had not been rising in line with those of U.S. chip makers.
"MPI is a bit downstream from wafer fabrication, so they are not so affected by the prices," said analyst Bernard Tan of Merrill Lynch Singapore Private Ltd.
